We combine ultra-fast laser scanning with recent time-gated 2D sensor arrays to capture the scene's impulse response on a visible relay wall. From the captured impulse response, our method computes an analogous virtual impulse response at any other hidden wall. This effectively allows us to concatenate a second, virtual NLOS imaging system that leverages higher-order illumination. We validate our cascaded imaging method both in simulation and with a real prototype, demonstrating NLOS imaging with fourth- and fifth-bounce illumination of objects in challenging orientations and hidden around two corners. We also analyze how wave-based NLOS imaging interacts with rough hidden walls, which explains and helps overcome existing visibility limitations. We further illustrate how to image hidden objects from different perspectives, thus observing previously unseen features, by relying on multiple hidden walls.

title: An ensemble approach driven by spatial interaction for modelling urban epidemic dynamics
abstract: Modelling spatial interactions remains a core issue in geographic information science. Faced with the emerging, non-stationary spread of epidemics, the effects and uncertainties of spatial interactions are amplified. Limited by reliance on a single spatial interaction prior, existing models perform well in specific scenarios but suffer from prediction drift across multi-phase epidemics, thereby hindering real-time and dynamic policy adjustments. To address this limitation, we propose an ensemble approach driven by spatial interaction, built upon a foundational metapopulation model. Using the 2022 Shanghai Omicron outbreak as a case study, we evaluated the proposed ensemble model against 14 mechanistic and machine learning baselines. In multi-phase prediction tasks, the proposed ensemble model achieves the best overall performance with mean ranks of 3.25 for RMSE and 4.00 for R2, surpassing all baselines with mean ranks ranging from 5 to 15. Furthermore, it improves mean predictive accuracy by 29% to 72% compared with the non-ensemble models, while reducing the prediction error interval by 10% to 84%. Finally, we generated model-based projections across multiple counterfactual scenarios to explore responses to changes in intervention timing and intensity.

title: A novel satellite embedding-driven SWOT framework for river discharge estimation: a case study of the Yangtze river
abstract: Accurate river discharge estimation is essential for water cycle modeling, water hazards prevention, water ecosystem protection and water resource management. However, conventional ground-based gauging networks are often sparsely distributed and insufficient to capture the complex hydrodynamic characteristics within large and heterogeneous river basins. With the rapid advancement of remote sensing technologies, particularly the launch of the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission, new opportunities have emerged for large-scale and continuous river discharge estimation. In this study, we develop and evaluate a SWOT-based river discharge estimation framework for the Yangtze River by integrating SWOT RiverSP hydraulic observations organized on the SWORD river network with Satellite Embedding V1 data in a random forest model to capture both hydrodynamic and geomorphological characteristics. The framework is evaluated using temporally separated training and testing observations from nine gauging stations along the Yangtze River mainstream, with station-specific nonlinear empirical models used for comparison. The main conclusions are as follows: 1) The random forest model substantially improves discharge estimation relative to the empirical formulation, with a maximum NSE gain of 0.4372 and an NRMSE reduction of up to 0.1175; 2) The model demonstrates reliable performance across the nine gauging stations, with all stations achieving NSE ≥ 0.72 and the overall performance reaching NSE = 0.8910 and NRMSE = 0.0664; 3) The spatially explicit discharge estimates show strong agreement with reach-scale results (correlation ≈ 0.9), indicating that water level exerts primary control on discharge, while channel width and geometry significantly modulate discharge responses in morphologically complex reaches. These results demonstrate the potential of combining SWOT hydraulics with satellite foundation embeddings to improve discharge estimation.

title: High-resolution forest height mapping across boreal and temperate forest sites using Hongtu-1 multistatic X-band TomoSAR
The hidden dimension: Resolving the vertical gradients of solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence emissions and gross primary production in modern maize canopy
Fusing a foundation model with spatiotemporal correction for automated long-term tracking of rift propagation from satellite imagery: a case study of the amery ice shelf
abstract: Long-term satellite monitoring of rift propagation is essential for assessing Antarctic ice shelf stability and projecting sea-level rise. Currently, long-term tracking of rifts still relies on time-consuming manual interpretation, significantly affecting its feasibility for large-scale rift monitoring. Here, we present a novel framework for automatically tracking rift propagation, which fuses the fine-tuned visual foundation model (Segment Anything Model, SAM) and spatiotemporal correction. The SAM enables automated rift extraction using only a few samples without any manual prompts, while the spatiotemporal correction improves the precision of rift mapping for geometric measurements. We applied this framework to automatically monitor key rifts on the Amery Ice Shelf using 768 Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 images from 2015 to 2025, achieving an F1 score of 98.6% across 11 independent scenes. Rift length and width measurements were in agreement with manual interpretation, with R2 values of 0.979 and 0.999, respectively. Furthermore, our extended monitoring revealed recent structural changes within the rift system on the Amery Ice Shelf. This study offers a new way for automated rift tracking with the foundation model for the first time, having significant potential for long-term monitoring of pan-Antarctic rifts.

A unified framework for estimation of daily mean land surface temperature from multiple MODIS observation combinations using Bayesian-optimized XGBoost model
Resolving the daytime NIRv rhythm of winter wheat under drought stress from Chinese geostationary FY-4A satellite observations
TS-PFDM: a temporally scaled probability-flow diffusion model for thick cloud removal in remote sensing images

title: PHYIELD: Towards multi-scale maize yield estimation with limited ground reference data via integrated crop models and phenology-guided deep learning
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurately estimating crop yields across scales (e.g., regional administrative and field scales) is critical for global food security, given mounting challenges agriculture faces from climate change, population growth, soil degradation, and water scarcity. Remote sensing has been widely used for crop yield estimation with its spatially extensive coverage and temporally continuous observations of crop conditions. However, robust yield estimation across scales remains challenging, particularly under conditions of limited availability of crop yield and crop management data. While process-based crop models can capture complex interactions of plant-soil-atmosphere continuum, their large-scale application is limited by computational cost, parameterization difficulty, and model input (e.g., management) constraints. Empirical data-driven models are more flexible and computationally efficient, but they heavily depend on ground-measured yield labels that are often scarce over space and time. To address these challenges, we propose PHYIELD, a novel hybrid yield estimation framework that integrates systematically calibrated process-based crop modeling and phenology-guided deep learning for maize yield estimation at both county and field scales under yield data constraint conditions. PHYIELD mainly comprises three components: systematic crop model calibration, diversified crop model simulation, and phenology-guided deep learning. Given the challenges and prevalence of sparse yield observations in practice, PHYIELD is uniquely devised with limited ground yield records for model building. Its model performance is systematically evaluated for temporal, spatial, and scale transfers, upon comparison with standalone crop model and deep learning counterpart benchmarks. Results showed that the systematic crop model calibration of PHYIELD, particularly via the calibration for Leaf Area Index (LAI), followed by yield (biomass multiplied by Harvest Index [HI]), is essential for region-varying parameterizations of the crop model before coupling with deep learning. With diversified simulations from calibrated crop model and phenology-guided deep learning, PHYIELD achieved correlation (R) of 0.53–0.73, bias of −1.47–0.96 t ha⁻ 1 , and root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.07–1.68 t ha⁻ 1 in the study region, outperforming both crop model and deep learning benchmarks. Under significant yield data constraint condition (e.g., only 2023 county-level yield data of Illinois available), PHYIELD demonstrated superior temporal transferability over the preceding 20 year period (2003–2022) (R = 0.70, RMSE = 1.76 t ha⁻ 1 ), spatial transfer to surrounding states (R = 0.85, RMSE = 1.06 t ha⁻ 1 ), and scale transfer from county to field levels (R = 0.53–0.76, RMSE = 1.55–1.58 t ha⁻ 1 ). By leveraging the complementary strengths of process-based and data-driven modeling approaches, coupled with systematic parameterization of crop model and incorporation of phenology knowledge, PHYIELD provides a more robust and generalizable solution for multi-scale maize yield estimation, particularly under limited data conditions. It can largely support yield-oriented decision-making in agricultural management, policy development, and food security planning.

title: Bathymetric imaging of rivers subject to ice cover: The Lena case
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing

title: Urban Architect: Steerable 3D Driving Scene Generation With Layout Prior
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Text-to-3D generation has achieved remarkable success via large-scale text-to-image diffusion models. Nevertheless, scaling this methodology to large-scale driving scenes is underexplored. Driving scenes, characterized by numerous elements, intricate arrangement relationships, and vast scale, present a formidable barrier to the interpretability of ambiguous textual descriptions for effective model optimization. In this work, we surmount the limitations by introducing a compositional 3D layout representation into text-to-3D paradigm, serving as an additional prior. It comprises a set of semantic primitives with simple geometric structures and explicit arrangement relationships, complementing textual descriptions and enabling steerable generation. Specifically, we represent the scene via 2D Gaussian splatting and develop two innovative optimization strategies: (1) Layout-Guided Variational Score Distillation, which addresses model optimization inadequacies by conditioning the score distillation sampling process with geometric and semantic constraints of 3D layouts; (2) Semantic-Depth Score Distillation Sampling, which ensures alignment of semantics, geometry, and appearance by matching the rendered semantic and depth maps with 3D layouts. Extensive experiments substantiate the capability of our framework to scale text-to-3D generation to large-scale driving scenes that cover over 1000 m driving distance for the first time. We also present various scene editing demonstrations, showing the powers of steerable urban scene generation.

title: Learning a Conceptual Space as a Bridge for Text-Video Retrieval
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: The goal of text-video retrieval is to learn a shared embedding space in which semantically relevant videos and texts have higher similarity. Recent advances employ contrastive learning to bring the paired video and text features closer. Despite these achievements, the inherent modality disparity, i.e., videos are detailed while texts are often brief, leads to the issues of incomplete correspondence and false negatives between video and text. These issues limit the effectiveness of existing contrastive learning approaches that rely on hard labels for direct text-video alignment. To this end, we present CoSTVR, a novel framework that introduces a conceptual space as a semantic bridge to enhance text-video feature alignment. Specifically, we regard concepts as a shared representation that bridges video and text modalities, and construct a conceptual codebook based on a set of concept prototypes. Building upon this codebook, we perform complementary concept-centered alignment in addition to direct text-video alignment. To implement concept-centered alignment from different feature granularities, we design token quantization and concept perception modules. Token quantization maps continuous patch-level and word-level features to discrete conceptual embeddings. Concept perception predicts the concepts present in video and text from global features, supervised by the concept labels we constructed. These two modules guide video and text features toward shared conceptual representations, grounding both modalities in a unified conceptual space. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of CoSTVR, achieving state of-the-art performance on three popular benchmarks, MSRVTT, DiDeMo, and ActivityNet Captions. Further ablation analysis shows that our method effectively mitigates the modality gap and enhances text-video alignment.

title: InfMasking: A Unified Variational Framework for Synergistic Multimodal Learning
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Multimodal models are expected to exploit synergistic information, that is, information available only when multiple modalities are observed together. In practice, however, a fusion module can fit the training objective by relying on a dominant modality or on information that modalities share, and the synergy between modalities is often left unused. We propose InfMasking, a unified multimodal learning framework based on Infinite Masking. Before fusion, InfMasking randomly masks the features of each modality; each sampled mask produces a different partial combination of cross-modal evidence and a fused representation of the corresponding modality interactions. All masked fused representations are required to remain consistent with a reference target: the unmasked fused view when training is unsupervised, and the class proxy of the task label when labels are available. Maintaining this consistency across diverse partial combinations discourages reliance on a dominant modality or on shared information alone, and drives the fusion module to learn crossmodal interaction patterns that remain meaningful under partial observations. Since the objective is an expectation over infinitely many masks, we model the masked fused representations as Gaussian and optimize closed-form variational bounds, whose population-moment gaps are controlled by the masking-induced covariance under this model. On the evaluated benchmarks, InfMasking improves predictive performance and yields higher mean PID estimates of task-label synergy in learned modalityspecific representations, alongside higher InterSHAP interaction attribution in the trained predictors.

title: Distilling Transformers: A Survey
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Transformers have gained widespread recognition across sectors and academic fields for their innovative self-attention mechanism, which effectively captures long-range dependencies, and for their scalability and exceptional performance across diverse applications. However, their high computational cost and time requirements limit their adoption in resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation provides a straightforward yet effective approach for compressing traditional network architectures, such as CNNs, by transferring knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. This paper explores the potential for model compression by combining novel Transformer architectures with knowledge distillation. Specifically, we categorize, summarize, and present the substantial body of work on Transformer knowledge and distillation schemes. Furthermore, this survey extends its coverage to widely used knowledge-distillation pipelines for large language models (LLMs) and systematically analyses six major distillation targets. We also review popular applications in various domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, and speech recognition. Finally, we provide forward-looking perspectives, highlighting potential directions for future research on developing highly efficient yet performance-competitive Transformer models through knowledge distillation techniques.

title: DepthGS: Depth-Guided Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Regularization for High-Quality Surface Reconstruction
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as an efficient representation for novel view synthesis, offering fast differentiable rendering and high visual fidelity, and has increasingly been extended to surface reconstruction. However, the relationship between depth information and reconstruction error remains insufficiently understood, limiting the principled design of geometric optimization strategies. To address this issue, we propose DepthGS, a depth-guided Gaussian splatting framework. We derive theoretical relations between depth discrepancies and reconstruction error under single-view and multi-view conditions. For single-view optimization, we propose a depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization strategy that modulates the normal constraint strength using a geometric reliability weight computed from local depth differences. For multi-view optimization, we introduce a cross-view depth consistency regularization strategy that enforces consistency between neighboring-view depth maps and the corresponding depth predictions transformed from the current view, thereby promoting multi-view geometric consistency. Extensive experiments on DTU, Mip-NeRF360, and Tanks and Temples demonstrate that DepthGS achieves competitive performance in both surface reconstruction and novel view synthesis.

title: MvP: Learning Motion Prior for Diffusion-Based 3D Human Pose Estimation
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Recent diffusion-based solutions for 3D Human Pose Estimation (HPE) leverage generative modeling to address depth ambiguity and uncertainty in 2D-to-3D lifting. While substantial progress has been made in spatial accuracy, the generation of temporally coherent trajectories remains largely underexplored, which is crucial for understanding realistic human motion. In this work, we propose to model a motion prior for temporally consistent joint trajectories, together with a pose prior for anatomically plausible 3D poses, through independent diffusion models. Specifically, we represent motion using relative joint displacements, defined as the positional differences of joints between frames. The motion prior thus refers to the distribution of relative joint-displacement sequences modeled by the displacement denoiser. Motivated by the observation that human joint motion is typically smooth over short time periods, we introduce a keyframe denoiser to estimate poses at uniformly sampled keyframes, which also serve as anchors for displacement accumulation. Accordingly, we decompose 3D HPE into keyframe estimation and displacement estimation. Two specialized denois ers with exchanged attention orders and independent objec tives are designed to capture spatial correlations and temporal dependencies, respectively. We further introduce an endpoint corrected pose aggregation scheme that accumulates predicted displacements while maintaining consistency between adjacent keyframes. Extensive evaluations on three widely used 3D HPE benchmarks, Human3.6M (H36M), MPI-INF-3DHP (3DHP), and the challenging in-the-wild 3DPW, demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in balancing spatial accuracy and temporal smoothness. Notably, MvP achieves competitive spatial accuracy under zero-shot evaluation and improved temporal consistency after adaptation to the target domain.

title: A spatiotemporal difference-enhancement network with semantic flow alignment for fine-grained cropland change detection
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Accurate cropland change detection from high-resolution remote sensing images is essential for agricultural resource monitoring, land management, and food security. Existing methods struggle with two primary challenges: (1) severe pseudo-change noise and false alarms, caused by sole reliance on simple spatial or temporal difference enhancement, and (2) inadequate fine-grained cropland change detection, resulting from boundary detail degradation during fixed interpolation decoding. To address these issues, we propose a S patio T emporal D ifference- E nhancement N etwork (STDENet) with semantic flow alignment for effective cropland change detection from high-resolution remote sensing images. Built on a pyramid vision transformer V2 (PVT-V2) encoder, STDENet integrates three key innovations: a spatiotemporal dual-branch difference enhancement (STDDE) module that jointly captures temporal variations and spatial discrepancies to suppress irrelevant responses from unchanged or spectrally similar regions; an adaptive boundary-aware (ABA) module that dynamically extracts four-directional texture cues to enhance boundary representations; and a semantic flow-aligned decoding (SFAD) module that predicts semantic flow fields to warp high-level difference features and align them with low-level spatial details for fine-grained structure recovery. We evaluate the STDENet on one self-constructed dataset, DYCD, and two public benchmark datasets, CLCD and Hi-CNA. Comparative experiments confirm that STDENet consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on all three datasets, improving IoU by 3.41 %, 4.90 %, and 1.98 % over the second-best methods on DYCD, CLCD, and Hi-CNA, respectively. By enhancing global structural information through the spatial branch and local change responses through the temporal branch, the spatiotemporal interaction design improves the feature separability of cropland changes. Semantic flow alignment helps restore fine-grained details by producing a more stable decoding process for local contours in cropland change patches. STDENet also demonstrates stronger resistance to interference and better adaptability to phenological variations among crop growth, pre-sowing, and post-harvest periods. Large-scale applications further indicate its generalization ability across heterogeneous cropland structures.

title: A multi-source remote sensing benchmark for event-level wildfire spread prediction in California using spatiotemporal deep learning
abstract: Satellite-based wildfire spread studies differ in data organization and evaluation procedures, making model performance difficult to compare. We constructed an event-level benchmark to compare model performance and examine how the models used the available inputs. The benchmark covers California during 2012 to 2021 and combines VIIRS 375 m active-fire observations, MODIS NDVI-derived vegetation information, and ERA5-Land wind fields. Each wildfire event was represented on a fixed 100 × 100 grid. Each sequence sample used ten historical daily steps to predict the next-day satellite-observed fire-state mask. Six spatiotemporal models (CNN-LSTM, Vision Transformer, ConvLSTM, Pairwise-ConvLSTM, Patchwise-ConvLSTM, and ST-GNN) were evaluated using common input definitions, preprocessing procedures, prediction targets, and metrics. Integrated Gradients was applied after training to quantify attributions from the five raster input channels to the next-day model outputs. Pairwise-ConvLSTM achieved the lowest overall RMSE of 0.0495 on the cumulative wildfire dataset. Among the five evaluated Patchwise-ConvLSTM configurations, the 7 × 7 setting achieved the highest observed F1-score (0.955), with precision (0.962) and recall (0.949). On the newly burned-pixel subset, the same configuration achieved precision (0.916), recall (0.888), and F1-score (0.902). The attribution analysis showed larger mean absolute values for vegetation-constrained unburned states (7.23 × 10−5) and prior cumulative fire history (5.13 × 10−5) than for newly detected fire pixels (1.81 × 10−5), the eastward wind component (7.01 × 10−6), and the northward wind component (8.97 × 10−6). The benchmark provides a common framework for assessing predictive performance and model input use in next-day satellite-observed wildfire spread prediction.

title: Vegetation restoration enhances drought resilience through threshold-dependent carbon–water regulation in a semi-arid sandy ecosystem
abstract: Drought increasingly constrains ecosystem functioning in semi-arid regions, yet the nonlinear thresholds through which vegetation restoration regulates carbon–water processes and ecosystem resilience remain poorly understood. In this study, a drought–carbon–water–resilience framework was developed to assess how vegetation restoration affects ecosystem drought resilience in the Mu Us Sandy Land, a representative semi-arid sandy ecosystem in northern China. MODIS products, including MOD17A2H/MOD17A3H for gross and net primary productivity (GPP and NPP), MOD16A2 for evapotranspiration (ET), MOD13A2 for the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), MOD11A2 for land surface temperature (LST), and MOD44B for vegetation cover, were used for the period 2001–2020 and harmonized to a 1000-m spatial resolution and an annual temporal scale to quantify water use efficiency (WUE), carbon use efficiency (CUE), the temperature–vegetation drought index (TVDI), ecosystem resistance, recovery, resilience, and a restoration intensity index (RII). The results showed that drought intensity increased slightly over time, while WUE and CUE exhibited contrasting spatial patterns and different sensitivities to drought. At the pixel scale, temporal correlations between annual TVDI and WUE/CUE were positive over 83.74% and 69.78% of the study area, respectively, indicating that carbon–water use efficiency often showed compensatory increases under mild-to-moderate drought conditions. In contrast, the regional drought-gradient analysis revealed threshold-dependent responses of WUE and CUE to increasing TVDI, with critical thresholds at approximately TVDI = 0.67 and TVDI = 0.66, respectively; beyond these thresholds, both water and carbon use efficiency declined rapidly. Strong restoration areas showed higher RSwue and RScue than weak/no restoration and degradation areas, and the proportion of high-resilience areas increased with restoration intensity, particularly for CUE-based resilience. Hierarchical regression further showed that RII provided additional explanatory power for ecosystem resilience after controlling for drought intensity, although its effects differed between water-use and carbon-use processes. These findings indicate that vegetation restoration enhances drought resilience through threshold-dependent carbon–water regulation, but its effectiveness depends on vegetation structure and water availability. Threshold-based monitoring and structure-optimized restoration should therefore be prioritized in semi-arid sandy ecosystem management.

title: The salinity-aridity nexus modulates eco-hydrological impacts of vegetation enhancement and desertification across saline-alkali drylands in northern China
abstract: Vegetation dynamics in drylands fundamentally restructure the land-atmosphere interface, yet the resulting surface water-energy coupling across saline-alkali environments remains insufficiently understood due to the complex interplay between climatic aridity and edaphic salinity. By integrating multi-decadal satellite observations with a biogeophysical decomposition framework, we quantified the growing-season impacts of vegetation enhancement (cropland expansion and grassland restoration) alongside desertification across the saline-alkali drylands of northern China from 2003 to 2020. Our results demonstrated that vegetation enhancement induced significant localized surface cooling, peaking in barren-to-cropland conversions (−0.674 ± 0.02 K), followed by grassland-to-cropland conversions (−0.066 ± 0.007 K) and barren-to-grassland restoration (−0.017 ± 0.009 K), whereas desertification exhibited a subtle warming tendency (+0.005 ± 0.0003 K). These thermal responses were primarily governed by non-radiative, evapotranspiration-mediated processes. Furthermore, the salinity-aridity nexus modulated regional energy partitioning through two divergent hydro-edaphic pathways. In reclaimed irrigated cropland, management interventions alleviated ambient matric and osmotic constraints, while intensifying regional water consumption. In contrast, non-irrigated restored grasslands exhibited a functional decoupling between canopy greening and evaporative cooling, reflecting conservative stomatal regulation enforced by compound soil matric and osmotic stresses. The marginal warming accompanying desertification indicated an impaired surface evaporative buffer following vegetation loss and secondary salinization. By elucidating how the salinity-aridity nexus modulates land-surface water-energy coupling, these findings highlight the necessity to align restoration strategies with local hydro-edaphic capacities, balancing the microclimatic cooling of irrigated agriculture against the long-term hydrological sustainability of natural grasslands under accelerating global change.

title: Hyper-Counter: Cross-Modal Hypergraph Fusion for RGB-T Crowd Counting
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: In RGB-T crowd counting, the performance of existing methods is often constrained by two major challenges. On the one hand, the inherent spatial misalignment between RGB and thermal infrared images makes cross-modal feature alignment and fusion extremely difficult. On the other hand, effectively integrating the complementary semantic information from both modalities and capturing their complex high-order associations remains a significant challenge. To address these issues, we propose Hyper-Counter, a novel framework based on crossmodal hypergraph fusion, introducing hypergraph learning into RGB-T crowd counting for the first time. Specifically, we utilize parallel Transformer backbones to extract multi-scale features and employ convolutional blocks to preliminarily fuse the features from both modalities into joint features. Subsequently, we design a cross-modal hypergraph perception module (CroM-HP), where feature patches are treated as vertices, and a cross-modal hypergraph is constructed based on the joint and cross-modal features. Hypergraph neural networks are then used to achieve efficient semantic information interaction and fusion. Through CroM-HP, the model can associate corresponding regions across modalities in a spatially flexible manner and effectively capture the intricate complementary semantic correlations. Moreover, a pyramid structure is adopted in the multi-level CroM-HPs to achieve cross-scale semantic transmission. Experiments on two widely used datasets, RGBT-CC and Drone-RGBT, demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms existing RGBT crowd counting methods. In particular, compared with the representative prior method BMCC on Drone-RGBT, Hyper- Counter improves the GAME(0) and RMSE metrics by 7.58% and 9.71%, respectively.

title: DepthShield: Optical Depth Encoding for Image Tampering Detection
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Detecting image forgeries is increasingly difficult as diffusion-based and manual edits preserve perceptually plausible image statistics. Most existing tampering detection methods rely solely on post-capture data, assuming a trusted acquisition process, and thus degrade when attackers replicate the image formation distribution. We introduce DepthShield, a depth assisted integrity framework that enforces authenticity at the moment of capture by coupling optical encoding with learned verification. The system operates in two coordinated stages that separate secure capture from high-quality release to end users. In the Image Capture Stage (IC-Stage), a designed phase mask modulates the image formation process to encode depth dependent signatures. This establishes a deterministic mapping between scene geometry and the encoded image, prioritizing security over initial visual quality (∼ 20 dB). Any unauthorized manipulation disrupts this fundamental RGB-Depth relationship. In the Integrity Restoration Stage (IR-Stage), a high-quality image (∼30 dB) is reconstructed from the protected capture and its depth cues while anchoring structural depth relationships necessary for reliable authentication. Rather than relying on statistical RGB artifacts only, DepthShield verifies whether an image is authentic by verifying the geometric consistency between the recovered RGB intensities and its corresponding depth map, as defined by the inverse mapping of the optical system. Experiments demonstrate that DepthShield surpasses software-only baselines across diverse tampering types, including diffusion-based edits, splicing, and local edits, and remains robust under common degradations such as compression. In addition, we implement a hardware prototype, validating its effectiveness on real-world captured scenes.

title: Revisiting Overestimation Bias of Q-learning: Breaking Bias Propagation Chains Does Well
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: This paper revisits the overestimation bias of Q-learning from a new perspective, i.e., the breaking bias propagation chains. We make five-fold contributions. First, we analyze the estimation bias propagation chains of Q-learning, and find that the bias propagated from previous steps dominates the maximum Q-value estimation bias and slows the convergence speed, instead of the current bias. Second, we propose a novel positive-negative bias alternating algorithm called Alternating Q-learning (AQ). It breaks the unidirectional estimation bias propagation chains via alternately executing Q-learning and Double Q-learning. We show theoretically that there exist suitable alternating parameters to eliminate the propagation bias. Third, we design an adaptive alternating strategy for AQ, obtaining Adaptive Alternating Q-learning (AdaAQ). It applies a softmax strategy with the absolute value of TD error to choose Q-learning or Double Q-learning for each state-action pair. Fourth, we extend AQ and AdaAQ to the large-scale settings with function approximation, i.e., including both discrete- and continuous-action Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). Fifth, both discrete-and continuous-action DRL experiments show that our method outperforms several state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines drastically; tabular MDP experiments reveal fundamental insights into why our method can achieve superior performance.

title: Remote sensing reveals vegetation-specific structure–function controls on carbon sequestration services in phenologically heterogeneous alpine ecosystems
Beyond spectral diversity: Spectral detection of dominant species decodes grassland plant diversity across management regimes
PACE hyperspectral observations enable a new paradigm for global mapping of terrestrial gross primary production
abstract: Accurate quantification of terrestrial gross primary production (GPP) is fundamental to understanding plant productivity, ecosystem function, and carbon-climate feedbacks. Existing approaches typically rely on meteorological, soil, and other ancillary inputs, which introduce substantial uncertainties at regional to global scales. NASA's Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission, carrying the Ocean Color Instrument (OCI), provides the first contiguous global hyperspectral observations from space. Using 122 spectral bands from PACE, we developed a data-driven framework based on partial least squares regression to generate an 8-day global GPP product. The model achieves a robust performance (R 2 = 0.71, RMSE = 1.93 gC m −2 d −1 ), comparable to models that incorporate meteorological drivers, and outperforms approaches based on broadband reflectance or vegetation indices. PACE-derived GPP showed broad spatial correspondence with solar-induced fluorescence (SIF), including hotspots across high productivity regions such as the U.S. Corn Belt, the Amazon and Congo basins, and the Indo-Gangetic and North China Plains. This strong spatial coherence supports the physiological relevance of the PACE retrievals. Our results demonstrate that hyperspectral observations provide a direct, observation-driven framework for estimating plant productivity at the global scale, opening new opportunities for monitoring vegetation responses to environmental change.

title: Assessing the detectability of standing dead trees in PlanetScope imagery
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Standing dead trees (SDTs) play a critical role in forest biodiversity assessment, disturbance monitoring, and carbon cycling. High-resolution optical satellite imagery offers an opportunity for large-scale SDT detection by providing finer spatial detail than moderate-resolution sensors. Despite this advantage, isolated SDTs may occupy only part of a PlanetScope pixel, allowing their signals to mix with those of live canopy, non-woody vegetation, and shadows. As a result, it is necessary to quantify signal detectability and detection stability across these conditions. To address this issue, this study uses PlanetScope imagery at 3 m resolution and Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV)-derived reference annotations to develop a multi-level, response-based SDT framework for analyzing SDT detectability from the aspect of the segmentation models, SDT density, and SDT patch sizes. UAV annotations are first aggregated to the PlanetScope pixel scale to generate hard labels and soft labels. The deep and machine learning models are then trained to select a stable reference semantic model and assess the consistency of SDT detection responses across architectures. All deep learning segmentation models produced consistent detectability responses, with HRNet achieving the best performance, with a binary F1 of 0.86. A single-pixel SDT signal became evident mainly when SDT cover proportion reached the 70 %-80 %, whereas neighborhood support lowered this change to a local SDT density of 20 %–30 %. Patch-level analysis indicated more stable detection for SDT patches larger than 90–180 m 2 . Furthermore, reliable PlanetScope detection is associated with SDT dominance, spatial aggregation, and high local SDT density . The proposed framework provides a detectability analysis approach for evaluating the stability of SDT detection in 3 m satellite imagery and the consistency of these responses across semantic segmentation models, linking high-resolution satellite imagery probability mapping with ultra-high-resolution UAV-based observations.

title: Satellite remote sensing of polar clouds: a review of cloud detection, phase identification, and microphysical property retrieval (2001–2025)
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Polar clouds play important roles in regulating the surface energy budget, atmospheric moisture cycle, precipitation, and sea-ice variability, while their occurrence, vertical structure, thermodynamic phase, and microphysical properties remain difficult to characterize consistently across the Arctic and Antarctic. Satellite remote sensing enables broad-scale monitoring of polar clouds, yet high-albedo snow and ice surfaces, weak cloud–surface thermal contrast, frequent temperature inversions, and persistent mixed-phase conditions make cloud detection and property retrieval substantially more difficult than at lower latitudes. This review synthesizes progress during the quarter-century 2001–2025 in polar cloud satellite remote sensing with a focus on satellite-based polar cloud detection, cloud phase identification, and microphysical retrieval. It first analyzes the synergistic monitoring capabilities of multi-source satellite sensors, including passive multispectral imagers, active radars and lidars, and microwave radiometers. It then explores in depth the evolution of cloud detection methods from static physical thresholds to deep learning algorithms that integrate spatial information and multimodal features. For cloud phase identification and microphysical retrieval, this paper reviews the physical principles and technical limitations of representative methods, including threshold and Lookup Table (LUT) methods, Optimal Estimation Method (OEM), variational and Bayesian retrievals, analytical and empirical methods, and machine-learning approaches, with particular attention to the challenges associated with ice–liquid phase partitioning and vertical heterogeneity in polar mixed-phase clouds. Finally, it identifies the deficiencies in current research regarding the application of far-infrared and high-frequency submillimeter-wave bands, the construction of full-spatiotemporal coverage observation networks, and the physical consistency of data-driven models, and outlines priorities for developing a continuous, multi-dimensional polar cloud monitoring system based on coordinated high- and low-orbit observations, recent and forthcoming satellite instruments, and physically constrained artificial intelligence.

title: Semantic-guided Causal Representation Learning for Personalized Visual Multiple Clustering
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Personalized visual multiple clustering aims to uncover multiple clustering solutions for image data based on user-specified perspectives. Existing methods typically use pre-trained Vision-Language Models to align image features with the perspective keywords for clustering. However, the pre-trained models fail to generate user-specified image representations due to the entanglement of features from different perspectives, thereby hindering the alignment between visual representations and the given keywords and ultimately degrading clustering performance. To address this, we propose Semantic-guided Causal Representation learning for Personalized Multiple Clustering (SCR-PMC), which disentangles different perspective features via semantic-guided image interventions, thereby obtaining causal visual representations for clustering. Specifically, we first construct a cross-modal structural causal model to reveal spurious correlations across different perspectives and identify the backdoor paths that affect visual representations. Following the principle of backdoor adjustment, we generate semantic-guided cross-modal confounder proxies carrying non-target perspective semantic information to construct intervention images. By enforcing representation and neighborhood consistency between the original images and their intervention images, we reduce the influence of non-target perspective factors and obtain causal visual representations. Finally, we use cross-modal alignment loss to learn optimal semantic representations that align with causal visual representations for clustering. Theoretical analysis further proves that SCR-PMC mitigates interference from non-target perspectives in target-specific representation learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SCR-PMC achieves competitive performance compared to existing methods on personalized visual multiple clustering tasks.

title: Invariance, Stability, and Diversity: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Domain Generalization
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Multimodal Domain Generalization (MMDG) aims to learn models that generalize to unseen domains under unpredictable, modality-dependent distribution shifts. Despite recent progress, existing methods often rely on heuristic fusion strategies and lack a unified theoretical perspective, limiting their robustness under domain shifts. In this paper, we identify three fundamental challenges in MMDG: (I) insufficient cross-domain invariance across individual modalities and cross-modal interaction subspaces; (II) instability induced by asynchronous modality degradation, through which unreliable modalities impair joint representations; and (III) limited representation diversity, which exacerbates source-target support mismatch. To characterize these challenges, we derive a generalization error bound for a stability-weighted ensemble of modality-wise hypotheses, revealing three corresponding factors: Invariance (Source-Source Divergence), Stability (Stability-Weighted Error), and Diversity (Target-Convex Hull Divergence). Guided by this analysis, we develop a unified nonlinear fusion framework comprising Multi-Granularity Adversarial Alignment to promote invariance across modality-specific, interaction, and fusion spaces, Stability-Aware Adaptive Learning to prioritize reliable modalities during source training and mitigate asynchronous degradation, and Manifold Expansion to increase normalized source-feature dispersion as a source-side regularizer. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that our framework achieves the best overall average rank across 43 transfer tasks on seven datasets spanning four task families and eight diverse modalities.

title: Text-to-Image Diffusion Sample Selector for Learning With Noisy Labels
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Large-scale datasets inevitably contain noisy labels, compelling deep neural networks to overfit and degrade in performance. Existing learning with noisy labels (LNL) approaches partially alleviate this through sample selection. However, selection processes themselves inherently rely on models trained on noisy data, which makes them prone to self-confirmation bias. To overcome this issue, we decouple sample selection from model training by proposing a Text-to-Image Diffusion Sample Selector (TIDS), which can provide a clean initial subset for downstream learning, even under various complex and extremely noisy conditions. Theoretically, we constrain the selection criteria by minimizing the generalization error bound in noisy environments to ensure the reliability of the selected samples and facilitate the effective training of robust models. Our proposed TIDS innovatively explores the semantic understanding capabilities of diffusion models. It estimates the label noise probability by evaluating the matching confidence between noisy textual labels and corresponding images, while capturing class information that more closely approximates the ground-truth. Therefore, TIDS enables a two-stage data cleaning process: correction and selection, both of which are single-step, generic preprocessing techniques that can work out of the box with most LNL methods to improve robustness. Furthermore, we design an efficient and lightweight training framework tailored to TIDS, achieving superior performance on both synthetic and real-world noisy datasets. Code for reproducing our experiments is available at https://github.com/SenyuHou/TIDS.

title: MindExplore+: Towards Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action System
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) is crucial for autonomous decision-making in embodied systems. While current methods have advanced single-skill abilities, their short-horizon capability limits applicability in real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, we propose MindExplore+, a hierarchical VLA system with cross-skill capabilities for long-horizon tasks in dynamic environments. By iteratively aligning task planning and action execution, this approach ensures excellent generalization across diverse real-world scenarios. In the reasoning layer, task specific chains of thought (CoT) are designed for planning long horizon task sequences and providing meta-action signals. In the acting layer, a simple but powerful Mixture of Policy Experts strategy is built inspired by signals and multimodal inputs for adaptively selecting skill experts and generating closed-loop action sequences. Also, it presents a lightweight Multimodal Diffusion Policy (MMDP) to enhance spatial perception by fusing multi-visual modality features. Besides, the pioneering memory mechanism establishes feedback between the reasoning and acting layers, facilitating adaptive execution of long-horizon tasks and real-time replanning. Notably, we create SandGo-1k and SandThink-21k, the first expert-level multimodal embodied dataset and CoT dataset tailored for sandy environments. To further improve efficiency in embodied tasks, we introduce a Biview Token Optimization (BTO) strategy. The method prunes redundant tokens based on a set of pivot tokens to ensure preserving diversity, then low-attention tokens are aggregated to ensure preserving task relevance while further reducing sequence length. MindExplore+ is 3.01× more successful than existing methods in unstructured and dynamic environments. Furthermore, by using BTO, it achieves a 1.64× speedup and reduces FLOPs to 18.85% of the original model, while maintaining competitive task performance.

title: OESTR: An orbit-encoding spatiotemporal reconstruction framework for joint daytime–nighttime FY-3D LST gap filling
Uncertainty as the key to interoperability: Traceable frameworks for space-based imaging spectroscopy
abstract: By the end of this decade, several space agencies and commercial operators will develop and launch the next generation of space-based Earth observation satellites. This paper focuses on imaging spectroradiometers, which measure solar radiation reflected by the Earth’s surface across the ultra-violet, visible and short-wave infrared spectral ranges using hyperspectral sensors. To enable interoperable use of datasets from this growing constellation of sensors, it is essential to understand and manage differences between the measurements of the same target under similar conditions. These differences arise from multiple factors: real variations due to instrument design (e.g., differing spectral responses or viewing geometries), differences in Level 1 processing approaches based on pre-flight and post-launch calibration strategies, differences in higher-level processing into biophysical quantities, and any residual biases between sensors caused by measurement or processing errors — some of which may not be fully captured in reported uncertainties. A consistent approach to the analysis and documentation of uncertainties supports intercomparison between datasets. By assessing whether measurements agree within the expected uncertainty associated with the comparison, or identifying and quantifying systematic deviations when they do not, it becomes possible to validate interoperability and diagnose discrepancies. This paper outlines key concepts for harmonising uncertainty analysis and reporting techniques across missions, including the use of structured uncertainty propagation frameworks such as uncertainty trees. The goal is to initiate a roadmap for understanding and quantifying uncertainties in a way that facilitates robust intercomparison of multiple space-based imaging spectroradiometer measurements.

title: Revealing the influence of volcanic plumes on lake water quality parameters derived using remote sensing methods
abstract: Satellite-derived observations of inland waters are widely used in environmental monitoring, often forming the basis of long-term analyses in the absence of continuous in situ measurements. However, the influence of transient atmospheric phenomena, such as volcanic plumes, on these datasets remains insufficiently quantified. We investigate the impact of volcanic plumes generated during the 2011–2012 eruption of Puyehue-Cordón Caulle, on the availability of remotely observed lake data (lake surface water temperature [LSWT], turbidity and chlorophyll-a) compiled from the ESA Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Lakes dataset. We subsequently extend the assessment of LSWT observations, combining these with coincident plume observations from the Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer (MISR) and the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), to identify the impacts of diffuse volcanic plumes on remote lake observations. Linear mixed-effects models assessed plume effects, while accounting for lake-specific variability during plume events. These findings indicate that while existing cloud masking removes LSWT observations in the presence of dense ash-rich plumes, diffuse volcanic plumes frequently remain undetected while significantly impacting LSWT records. Plume impacts varied seasonally, with LSWT observations being lower in winter months, and warmer in summer. At the pixel scale, plume interference was associated with LSWT8 reductions of up to 12 °C beneath dense ash-plumes, and 1 °C–5 °C beneath diffuse plumes. Geographic conditions influenced overall data availability, with measurable effects extending to ~270 km from the volcanic source. A random forest classification achieved an overall accuracy of 78% classification accuracy for distinguishing plumes from cloud and background regions, demonstrating the potential to develop an automated flag for CCI Lake data. These findings demonstrate that diffuse volcanic plumes can introduce substantial uncertainty into satellite-derived LSWT observations, although the magnitude and spatial extent of the observed effects are case-specific. This highlights the need for further investigation across diverse volcanic events and geographical settings to support the development of dedicated quality flags for diffuse and transient aerosol features.

title: A transferable satellite-derived bathymetry model without site-specific calibration for Case-1 optically shallow waters using Sentinel-2/MSI imagery
abstract: Accurate bathymetry in optically shallow waters (OSWs), particularly across coral reef environments, is essential for coastal ecosystem management and benthic habitat monitoring. Satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) offers a scalable alternative, but reliance on in situ depth measurements constrains its application in data-sparse OSW regions, while the coupling between water-column and benthic signals limits retrieval accuracy. Here, we developed OSW-SDB, a simulation-based SDB model for Case-1 OSWs that is not tailored to a specific region and accounts for variations in benthic reflectance. Using a newly developed benthic reflectance library comprising 2,100 spectra, we generated 200,000 pairs of water depth and remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) by radiative transfer simulations spanning diverse water-column optical properties and benthic reflectance conditions. An XGBoost model was trained based on the simulated dataset using SHAP-selected multispectral features, with 6,711 matched ICESat-2/ATL24 observations additionally used for hyperparameter optimization. OSW-SDB achieved coefficient of determination (R2) values above 0.96 and root mean square error (RMSE) values below 1 m on the simulated training and testing datasets. Two independent simulation-based validations using benthic spectra excluded from model development yielded R2 values of 0.84 and 0.94, and RMSEs of 2.26 and 1.35 m, respectively. Median absolute percentage errors (MdAPEs) were below 15% across all simulated datasets. This model was applied to Sentinel-2/MSI imagery after OSW extraction, producing spatially coherent 10-m bathymetry maps across seven OSW regions. Independent validation using 13,296 ATL24 depths covering 20 reef sites yielded an R2 of 0.80, an RMSE of 0.75 m, and an MdAPE of 26.13%. Additional evaluations using airborne LiDAR and in situ SeaBASS observations, together with comparisons against two existing SDB models, demonstrated stable performance across geographically diverse OSWs. The model is designed for Case-1 OSWs shallower than 20 m, with better performance below 10 m, consistent with the depth range of benthic habitat mapping. OSW-SDB enables practical and transferable bathymetric mapping at 10-m resolution across diverse Case-1 OSWs using only Sentinel-2/MSI imagery, without requiring site-specific bathymetric or benthic priors during application.

title: SparScene: Efficient Traffic Scene Representation via Sparse Graph Learning for Large-Scale Trajectory Generation
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Multi-agent trajectory generation is a core problem for autonomous driving and intelligent transportation systems. However, efficiently modeling the dynamic interactions between numerous road users and infrastructures in complex scenes remains an open problem. Existing methods typically employ distance-based or fully connected dense graph structures to capture interaction information, which not only introduces a large number of redundant edges but also requires complex and heavily parameterized networks for encoding, thereby resulting in low training and inference efficiency, limiting scalability to large and complex traffic scenes. To overcome the limitations of existing methods, we propose SparScene, a sparse graph learning framework designed for efficient and computationally scalable traffic scene representation. Instead of relying on distance thresholds, SparScene leverages the lane graph topology to construct structure-aware sparse connections between agents and lanes, enabling efficient yet informative scene graph representation. SparScene adopts a lightweight graph encoder that efficiently aggregates agent-map and agent-agent interactions, yielding compact scene representations with substantially improved efficiency and inference scalability. On the motion prediction benchmark of the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, SparScene achieves competitive performance with remarkable efficiency. It generates trajectories for more than 200 agents in a scene within 5 ms and scales to more than 5,000 agents and 17,000 lanes with merely 54 ms of inference time with only 2.9 GB of GPU memory, highlighting its superior computational scalability for large-scale traffic scenes.

title: Advancing remote sensing of carbon fractions in coastal waters: retrieval algorithms and optical proxies for Sentinel-2 MSI and Sentinel-3 OLCI
abstract: A thorough understanding of the global carbon pools and cycle is essential for understanding and predicting the effects of climate change. Coastal waters play a key role in the global carbon cycle but remain poorly understood due to their optical complexity, high spatial variability, and sensitivity to climate change. Satellite remote sensing data can provide high spatial and temporal resolution for carbon monitoring at local, regional, and global scales. This study estimates the potential of Sentinel-2 MSI (S2) and Sentinel-3 OLCI (S3) for mapping carbon fractions in coastal waters. In situ hyperspectral reflectance measurements and concentrations of different carbon fractions, namely Total Organic Carbon (TOC), Dissolved Organic Carbon (DOC), Particulate Organic Carbon (POC), and Dissolved Inorganic Carbon (DIC), were used. Bio-optical and physical water parameters, as well as carbon fractions, were measured in the coastal areas of the eastern Baltic Sea from 2023 to 2024. In situ reflectance spectra were recalculated to S2 and S3 band reflectance using their respective spectral response functions. Regression models, including linear regression and machine learning methods, were developed and validated against in situ data to estimate carbon fractions. For S2, the combinations of green and red or red-edge bands achieved the best performance in carbon retrieval, with R 2 values of 0.67, 0.64, and 0.56 for TOC, DOC, and DIC, respectively. The corresponding MAPE values ranged from 14% to 18%, and biases were close to zero. Slightly higher accuracies were obtained with S3 simulations. The S3 models that used reflectance at 490, 620, and 665 nm produced the most accurate estimates for both TOC ( R 2 = 0.71) and DOC ( R 2 = 0.67). For DIC, the best predictive model combined information from 510, 665, and 709 nm bands, achieving R 2 of 0.62. Among the tested optical proxies, CDOM absorption at 443 nm showed the most consistent relationship with TOC, DOC, and DIC ( R 2 = 0.56–0.30). The study represents a significant step forward in the remote sensing of coastal waters, and if adopted, the proposed carbon-fraction products could enable substantial progress across various fields, from carbon-cycle research to monitoring and policymaking.
